cards.back: A class that extends a server's capabilities and handles requests in a request-response model
cards.extra: It runs inside a servlet container, which manages its lifecycle and turns HTTP requests into Java objects.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::09 Build and Frameworks::06 Web Frameworks

cards.front: What are the three stages of a servlet's life cycle?
cards.extra: The container calls them; the servlet object lives between init and destroy, serving many requests concurrently.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::09 Build and Frameworks::06 Web Frameworks

cards.back: On the first request to that servlet — or at server startup if it is configured to load eagerly
cards.extra: It runs once, not per request. That is why per-request state must not be stored in servlet fields.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::09 Build and Frameworks::06 Web Frameworks

cards.back: Inspects the HTTP method and dispatches to doGet, doPost, doPut and so on
cards.extra: You normally override the do* methods and leave service() alone.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::09 Build and Frameworks::06 Web Frameworks

cards.back: Before the servlet is taken out of service — at context shutdown or reload
cards.extra: It is the place to release resources. After that the object is only waiting for the garbage collector.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::09 Build and Frameworks::06 Web Frameworks

cards.front: How do you write a servlet?
cards.extra: HttpServlet already implements the interface and the HTTP plumbing, so you override doGet/doPost only.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::09 Build and Frameworks::06 Web Frameworks

cards.back: Java Enterprise Edition — the set of enterprise specifications built on top of Java SE
cards.extra: It targets server-side needs: web components, transactions, messaging and persistence, running inside an application server.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::09 Build and Frameworks::06 Web Frameworks

cards.back: An open-source unit testing framework for Java
cards.extra: It provides annotations to mark tests and assertions to compare expected with actual values.

cards.front: What is a unit in unit testing?
cards.back: The smallest piece of code that can be tested in isolation — usually one method
cards.extra: Tests exercise that piece directly, without the database, network or UI around it.

cards.front: How does a JUnit assertion look?
cards.back: assertEquals(expected, actual) — it fails the test when the two differ
cards.extra: JUnit 5's Assertions class offers assertTrue, assertNull, assertThrows and more.

cards.back: The collection of prewritten classes, interfaces and methods shipped with the JDK, organised into packages
cards.extra: System.out.println and ArrayList are API calls: someone else wrote and tested that code.

cards.back: A number equal to the sum of its digits each raised to the power of the number of digits
cards.extra: 153 has three digits: 1³ + 5³ + 3³ = 1 + 125 + 27 = 153. Also called a narcissistic number.

cards.back: A number greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself
cards.extra: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11… The test is to try divisors up to the square root — beyond that, any factor would have a matching one below.

cards.front: Which framework does Simplilearn call the most widely used Java framework?
cards.back: Spring — described as lightweight, for design, development and deployment
cards.extra: Spring Boot builds on it to remove most configuration; the collection's Spring Boot deck covers that.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::09 Build and Frameworks::07 Spring Boot
